summary: You produced a working brute-force solution that passed all visible tests, but it failed one hidden test due to performance (the constraints explicitly require better than O(n^2)). The biggest gap was complexity reasoning: you stated the nested loops are O(n), and concluded no improvements were needed, which is the opposite of what this problem is designed to assess at scale.

test_results.summary_note: All visible tests passed (6/6), but 1 hidden test failed (3/4), consistent with the O(n^2) approach timing out on a large input.

dimensions.name: Correctness & Completeness
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: Your implementation returns correct indices when it finds a valid pair and avoids using the same element twice by starting j at i+1. It also correctly returns an empty list when no pair is found (even though the prompt guarantees one exists).
dimensions.what_to_improve: It did not fully satisfy the problem constraints because one hidden test failed; given the constraint up to 1e5, correctness includes meeting runtime requirements. Also, the empty-input guard is unnecessary under the stated constraints (nums.length >= 2), which suggests not fully anchoring to the spec.

dimensions.name: Problem-Solving & Thinking
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You quickly arrived at a straightforward baseline and validated it against the visible tests.
dimensions.what_to_improve: You did not pivot to a constraint-appropriate strategy (hash map / one-pass complement lookup) despite being asked about large inputs, and you stated there was nothing to improve. For interviews, demonstrating you can move from baseline to optimal is key, especially for a canonical problem like Two Sum.

dimensions.name: Technical Communication
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: You clearly described the brute-force idea upfront (scan the rest for the complement) and mentioned guarding against empty input.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Your complexity explanation was incorrect: you repeatedly asserted O(n) despite having nested loops, and you didn’t engage with the interviewer’s prompt about scale. A stronger response would explicitly acknowledge O(n^2), connect it to the 1e5 constraint, and propose an O(n) alternative.

dimensions.name: Complexity & Optimization
dimensions.label: needs work
dimensions.what_went_well: You used O(1) extra space, which is true for the brute-force approach.
dimensions.what_to_improve: The time complexity is O(n^2), not O(n). The answer key explicitly warns about staying at O(n^2) when O(n) is required; that appears to be the reason for the hidden failure. You also claimed the solution was already optimal, missing the standard O(n) hash map approach (time O(n), space O(n)).

dimensions.name: Code Quality
dimensions.label: adequate
dimensions.what_went_well: The code is simple, readable, and avoids index mistakes (correct loop bounds and early return).
dimensions.what_to_improve: Given the constraints, the implementation choice is the main quality issue: a clean, well-factored O(n) solution is expected. Also consider aligning behavior with the spec (exactly one valid answer exists), e.g., not needing to return [] for “not found” in a production interview setting unless the signature requires it.

dimensions.name: Independence
dimensions.label: strong
dimensions.what_went_well: You implemented your chosen approach without needing any hints.
dimensions.what_to_improve: Independence is strongest when paired with correct self-correction: when prompted about complexity and large inputs, you stayed committed to an incorrect analysis rather than reassessing.

thinking_and_logic: Your approach was a classic brute-force pair search: for each index i, scan all later indices j and return the first pair summing to target. The reasoning gap was in complexity: nested loops imply roughly n(n-1)/2 checks in the worst case, which is quadratic and will not meet the 1e5 constraint. When asked directly, you treated the inner loop as “part of processing each element,” but that processing still sums to O(n^2) overall.
code_assessment: Functionally, the implementation is correct for small/medium inputs and correctly avoids reusing the same element by enforcing j > i. However, the hidden failure indicates the solution does not satisfy performance requirements. The code is otherwise clean and straightforward; the main issue is algorithm selection relative to constraints.

next_steps.action: Practice converting a brute-force baseline into an optimal solution when constraints demand it
next_steps.why: Many interviews grade heavily on recognizing when O(n^2) won’t scale and producing the standard O(n) approach.
next_steps.how: For Two Sum: maintain a dict from value -> index. For each x at index i, check if (target - x) is already in the dict; if yes return [dict[comp], i]; otherwise store x:i. Then rehearse explaining why this is O(n) time, O(n) space.

next_steps.action: Drill complexity analysis for nested loops and common patterns
next_steps.why: Incorrect Big-O analysis was a core issue here and directly contradicted the interviewer prompts.
next_steps.how: For each problem you do, write down worst-case operation counts. For nested loops, explicitly sum iterations (e.g., sum_{i=0..n-1} (n-i-1) = O(n^2)). Say it out loud during practice.

next_steps.action: Build a habit of anchoring to constraints/spec before finalizing
next_steps.why: You added an unnecessary empty-input guard and concluded “already optimal” despite constraints explicitly warning about O(n^2).
next_steps.how: Before coding: restate constraints and required complexity. After coding: sanity-check algorithm against max input size (e.g., 1e5 => O(n^2) ~ 1e10 ops is infeasible).

patterns_to_study: time complexity of nested iteration (triangular sums)
encouragement: You’re close on implementation fundamentals—focus on Big-O accuracy and constraint-driven optimization, and this becomes an easy full-pass problem.

transcript.text: Here's the problem: given an array of integers and a target, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target.
Simple enough. I'll iterate through the array and for each element scan the rest for the complement. I'll also guard the empty input case.
Done. All the visible tests pass on the first run.
Nice. Can you analyze the complexity of your solution?
It's O(n) — I only have one main loop over the array, the inner scan is just part of processing each element. Space is O(1).
Are you confident about that time bound for large inputs?
Yes, linear. It only touches each element once from the outer loop's perspective.
Alright. Anything you'd improve given more time?
Not really, I think this is already optimal.
